To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mind change complexity of learning logic programs is in the range of the ordinal numbers ω, ω2, ωω, and ωωω, depending on the learning model, the class of programs and the number of facts.

1) the mind change complexity of learning minimal models of logic programs of length at most n is O(log n); 2) the same complexity bound is valid for learning minimal models that are also models of a fixed set of positive facts; and 3) the mind change complexities of learning minimal models and minimal models that are models of a fixed number of positive and negative facts are O(log2 n).

1) The mind change complexity of learning minimal models of bounded length logic programs is bounded from above by a function that is exponential in the length of the program, but polynomial in the number of atoms in the language.

the mind change complexity of learning minimal models of a logic program is determined by the mind change complexity bounds on the learning of the positive and the negative examples.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mind change complexity of learning minimal models of logic programs is a natural generalization of mind change complexity of inductive inference.
we have established ordinal mind change complexity for learnability of minimal models of length bounded logic programs both from positive and negative examples.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the mind change complexity of learning minimal models of logic programs from positive and negative examples is the same as the complexity of learning minimal Herbrand models.
, in general, learning from negative facts is harder than learning from positive facts.

, while learning minimal models of bounded length logic programs from positive facts is possible with a polynomial number of mind changes, learning from positive and negative examples requires a superpolynomial number of mind changes.
